choices: Reimage all 20 with a USB stick — Autopilot requires a custom image
Collect each device's hardware hash (for example with the Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo script) and import the CSV into Intune, then assign an Autopilot deployment profile
Manually create computer accounts in Microsoft Entra ID
Ship the laptops back — Autopilot only works with devices bought through specific resellers
scenarios.hint: What unique fingerprint does Autopilot use to recognize a device?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct way to get the missing devices into Autopilot?
scenarios.situation: Fifty new laptops arrived for Autopilot deployment, but only 30 appear under Devices > Windows > Windows enrollment > Devices in Intune. The missing 20 were never registered.
scenarios.title: The hash that wasn't there
scenarios.why: Autopilot identifies devices by their hardware hash, which must be registered in Intune before the out-of-box experience can pick up the deployment profile. The Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo script collects the hash into a CSV you import; partner-registered devices skip this step, but any device can be registered manually this way.

choices: Autopilot cannot do zero-touch — image the kiosks manually
The wrong deployment profile is assigned — create a self-deploying mode profile (no user interaction) and target the kiosk device group
The tablets need local admin accounts created first
Disable the Enrollment Status Page to skip provisioning
scenarios.hint: Which profile mode exists specifically for devices nobody signs into?
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong, and what fixes it?
scenarios.situation: Kiosk tablets are getting the standard user-driven Autopilot profile, so each one stops at a sign-in screen nobody can complete. They need to provision themselves with no user interaction.
scenarios.title: Profile roulette
scenarios.why: Autopilot deployment profiles define the out-of-box experience: user-driven profiles expect a person to sign in, while self-deploying mode provisions with no user interaction — the kiosk pattern. Profiles target device groups (devices have no user yet at assignment time), so the fix is a self-deploying profile assigned to the kiosk group.

choices: Windows Autopilot — it works fully offline
A provisioning package (.ppkg) built with Windows Configuration Designer, applied from USB — designed for offline, repeatable provisioning
Intune remote wipe — it reinstalls everything
Manual setup on each PC — the only offline option
scenarios.hint: Which provisioning method was built for sneakernet?
scenarios.prompt: Which provisioning method fits?
scenarios.situation: A remote site has no reliable internet and 15 PCs to provision identically: Wi-Fi profile, a local admin account, and three certificates. Shipping them to HQ is not an option.
scenarios.title: The USB stick rollout
scenarios.why: Provisioning packages (.ppkg) created in Windows Configuration Designer apply settings, accounts, certs, and apps at first boot or by double-click — no network needed, perfectly repeatable from a USB stick. Autopilot fundamentally requires cloud connectivity during OOBE, so it is the wrong tool for an offline site.

choices: Retire — it removes the device from Intune
Wipe — full factory reset, slowest, and it can remove Autopilot registration
Autopilot Reset — strips user data and settings, keeps the Autopilot registration, and re-runs OOBE for the next user
Fresh Start — keeps user data while reinstalling Windows
scenarios.hint: Which action was designed for 'next user, same device'?
scenarios.prompt: Which remote action is the best fit?
scenarios.situation: An employee left and their corporate laptop goes to a new hire. IT wants it clean and re-provisioned through Autopilot as fast as possible, keeping the Autopilot registration intact.
scenarios.title: Wipe vs Reset vs Fresh Start
scenarios.why: Autopilot Reset is purpose-built for device handoff: it removes personal files, apps, and settings, preserves the Autopilot registration and any provisioned apps, and drops the device back into the out-of-box experience. Wipe is heavier and can drop the registration; Retire only unenrolls without cleaning; Fresh Start keeps user data — wrong for a departing employee.

choices: Run Windows Update — it upgrades editions automatically
Use subscription activation: assign Microsoft 365 E3/E5 licenses and the devices step up from Pro to Enterprise automatically on next check-in
Buy retail Enterprise keys and type them into each PC
Deploy an Enterprise image over the network to each machine
scenarios.hint: What in Microsoft 365 already entitles the user to Enterprise?
scenarios.prompt: How do you upgrade the edition without reimaging?
scenarios.situation: Two hundred PCs run Windows Pro but the security baseline requires Windows Enterprise features. Reimaging 200 machines is off the table.
scenarios.title: Pro to Enterprise overnight
scenarios.why: Subscription activation upgrades Windows Pro to Enterprise based on the user's Microsoft 365 E3/E5 license — no key entry, no reimage. The device checks in, sees the entitlement, and steps up the edition. This is the cloud-era answer to edition upgrades and a staple of modern deployment.

choices: Disable the Enrollment Status Page entirely
Investigate the blocking app — a 2.1 GB MSI that fails install will hold ESP until timeout; fix or remove it from the ESP blocking list
Increase the ESP timeout to 4 hours
Tell users to wait longer
evidence:
ESP status: failed at 'Installing apps'
Blocking app: line-of-business MSI, 2.1 GB
scenarios.hint: What is ESP waiting for that never arrives?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most productive first troubleshooting step?
scenarios.situation: New Autopilot devices hang on the Enrollment Status Page for 40 minutes, then time out. Users are stuck staring at 'Setting up your device.'
scenarios.title: The ESP that never ends
scenarios.why: ESP blocks device setup until its required apps, policies, and certificates complete — a failing blocking app is the classic hang. The fix is at the app: repair the installer, or remove it from the ESP's blocking-apps list so setup completes and the app retries later. Raising the timeout just makes users wait longer for the same failure.

choices: Thicker images with more apps baked in
Modern provisioning: ship the OEM image, then Autopilot + Intune apply profiles, apps, and policies dynamically per device group
Manual setup checklists for each department
Keeping one image but updating it monthly
scenarios.hint: What if the 'image' never needed rebuilding because nothing was baked into it?
scenarios.prompt: What is the modern replacement for monolithic imaging?
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants to retire the golden-image process: every image rebuild takes weeks and drivers drift. They ask what replaces imaging in a cloud-managed world.
scenarios.title: Imaging is dead, long live provisioning
scenarios.why: Modern provisioning treats the factory OEM image as the starting point and layers configuration dynamically: Autopilot picks the right profile, Intune pushes apps and policies by group. No image maintenance, no driver injection marathons, and each department gets its own experience from the same base. That is the core mindset shift MD-102 tests.

choices: Microsoft Entra joined — full device management
Hybrid Microsoft Entra joined — for on-premises domain devices
Microsoft Entra registered — workplace join for personal/BYOD devices, enabling app-level (MAM) control without full enrollment
No identity needed — email works without it
scenarios.hint: Which identity says 'this is a personal device with a work account on it'?
scenarios.prompt: Which Microsoft Entra ID device identity fits?
scenarios.situation: A consultant's personal iPad needs access to corporate email with app-level protection, but IT must not manage or wipe the whole device.
scenarios.title: Joined, hybrid, or registered?
scenarios.why: Microsoft Entra registered (workplace join) is the BYOD identity: the user adds a work account to a personal device, enabling Conditional Access and app protection policies without Intune enrollment or device wipe. Entra joined implies corporate management; hybrid is for domain-joined machines syncing to the cloud.

choices: The devices need the Intune Company Portal installed first
Automatic enrollment is not enabled — in Microsoft Entra ID, Mobility (MDM and MAM) must have the MDM user scope set to Microsoft Intune for the right users
Autopilot profiles do not support automatic enrollment
The laptops must be hybrid joined instead
scenarios.hint: Which Entra ID setting connects 'joined' to 'managed'?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely missing configuration?
scenarios.situation: New laptops join Microsoft Entra ID successfully, but none appear in Intune. The Intune admin insists enrollment 'should be automatic.'
scenarios.title: The MDM scope nobody set
scenarios.why: Entra join and Intune enrollment are separate steps joined by automatic enrollment: Entra ID's Mobility (MDM and MAM) blade defines which users' devices auto-enroll into Intune (the MDM user scope). If the scope is None, devices join Entra ID and stop there — exactly this symptom. The Company Portal is for user-initiated enrollment, not the automatic path.

choices: Require multi-factor authentication
Require device to be marked as compliant — Intune compliance policies evaluate health and Conditional Access blocks the noncompliant
Require hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device
Block all mobile devices
scenarios.hint: Which grant control asks Intune for the device's health verdict?
scenarios.prompt: Which Conditional Access grant control enforces this?
scenarios.situation: Security wants only healthy devices reaching Exchange Online: encrypted, patched, with Defender running. Unhealthy devices must be blocked at sign-in.
scenarios.title: Compliant or else
scenarios.why: 'Require device to be marked as compliant' is the Conditional Access grant that consumes Intune compliance policy results: encryption on, OS version current, Defender healthy → compliant → access granted. Anything else is blocked or limited. MFA proves the user; compliance proves the device — this scenario is about the device.

choices: The device is fully managed — enrollment succeeded
The device is Entra joined but NOT enrolled in MDM — the MdmUrl is blank, so check the automatic enrollment scope
The device is hybrid joined — DomainJoined should be YES
The device failed Entra join — AzureAdJoined is misleading
evidence:
AzureAdJoined : YES
DomainJoined : NO
MdmUrl : (blank)
DeviceAuthStatus : SUCCESS
scenarios.hint: Which field proves the device talks to an MDM authority?
scenarios.prompt: What does this output tell you?
scenarios.situation: A laptop's Intune enrollment keeps failing. You run dsregcmd /status on the device to check its identity state.
scenarios.title: dsregcmd tells the truth
scenarios.why: dsregcmd /status is the ground truth for device identity: AzureAdJoined YES confirms cloud join, DomainJoined NO rules out hybrid, and a blank MdmUrl proves no MDM enrollment happened. DeviceAuthStatus SUCCESS means authentication works — so the join is fine and the gap is enrollment, pointing back at the MDM user scope.

choices: Enable MFA per-user in the Microsoft 365 admin center for each admin
Create a Conditional Access policy targeting the admin roles/users, grant control 'Require multifactor authentication', and exclude the break-glass emergency accounts
Require compliant devices for admins — that replaces MFA
Turn on Security Defaults and call it done
scenarios.hint: Which accounts must survive even a broken policy?
scenarios.prompt: How do you implement this with Conditional Access?
scenarios.situation: After a phishing wave, leadership mandates MFA for all administrator accounts accessing any cloud app. There must be no exceptions except emergency access accounts.
scenarios.title: MFA for the admins
scenarios.why: Conditional Access is the policy engine: target the admin population, require MFA as the grant control, and exclude break-glass emergency access accounts (which stay MFA-free by design so a CA misconfiguration can never lock out all admins). Per-user MFA is the legacy approach; Security Defaults cannot scope exclusions.

choices: Compliance policies enforce automatically — this one is broken
Configure Actions for noncompliance: notify the user immediately, then escalate (e.g., remotely lock or retire the device) after a grace period
Delete and recreate the policy
Compliance only reports; enforcement is impossible
scenarios.hint: A verdict with no consequence is just trivia — where do consequences live?
scenarios.prompt: What makes a compliance policy actually enforce consequences?
scenarios.situation: A compliance policy marks 40 devices noncompliant for missing encryption — but nothing happens. Users ignore the warnings and keep working.
scenarios.title: The compliance policy that cried wolf
scenarios.why: A compliance policy without actions is just a report. 'Actions for noncompliance' define the escalation: email the user at day 0, mark noncompliant, then remotely lock or retire after N days. Combined with Conditional Access requiring compliance, noncompliant devices lose resource access — that is the enforcement loop.

choices: Autopilot profiles must target device groups — at OOBE time there is no signed-in user, so user-group membership cannot be evaluated
User groups work fine — the profile is corrupt
Autopilot profiles cannot be assigned at all
The devices need to be Entra registered first
scenarios.hint: Who is 'logged in' during the out-of-box experience?
scenarios.prompt: Why did the assignment fail?
scenarios.situation: An Autopilot profile assigned to a user group never applies: devices sit at OOBE with no profile. The admin is confused because 'the users are in the group.'
scenarios.title: Device groups vs user groups
scenarios.why: During the out-of-box experience no user has signed in yet, so the device cannot resolve user-group membership. Autopilot profiles, ESP settings, and other pre-user configurations must target Microsoft Entra device groups. User groups are for policies that apply after sign-in (apps, some configs).

choices: One policy: conditions include the payroll app and a named location for the office IP ranges; grant requires compliant device OR trusted location, otherwise block
Block the payroll app's URL at the firewall
Require MFA only — location does not matter
Two separate tenants, one per location
scenarios.hint: Which CA element represents 'the office network' as a signal?
scenarios.prompt: Which Conditional Access pieces combine to enforce this?
scenarios.situation: Finance staff should access the payroll app only from the corporate office network or compliant devices. Access from elsewhere must be blocked.
scenarios.title: Location, location
scenarios.why: Conditional Access combines signals: the target resource (payroll app), network conditions (named locations built from trusted office IP ranges), and grant controls (require compliant device, or block). The policy expresses 'payroll app + not from office + not compliant = block' in one place — firewalls cannot see the user or device identity.

choices: Set deadlines to 0 — deadlines cause reboots
Add a grace period (e.g., 2-3 days) so users can schedule the restart, keep a firm deadline, and use active hours to avoid work hours
Disable Windows Update for Business entirely
Defer quality updates 30 days — deferral replaces deadlines
evidence:
Quality update deferral: 0 days
Deadline: 2 days
Grace period: 0 days
Auto restart: default
scenarios.hint: Which setting is the 'snooze button' between deadline and forced reboot?
scenarios.prompt: What update ring settings fix the user experience without losing control?
scenarios.situation: Windows Update for Business pushes quality updates with a 2-day deadline and no grace period. Users get force-rebooted mid-presentation.
scenarios.title: Update ring roulette
scenarios.why: Deadlines enforce compliance; the grace period is the human part — it gives users days to reboot on their terms after the deadline passes before the device forces it. Active hours keep restarts out of the workday. Deferral only delays when the update is offered; it does not soften the reboot.

choices: Faster rings — speed prevents breakage
Ring-based rollout: pilot group first, then broad deployment; update rings assigned to staged groups so issues surface on a few devices before hundreds
Manual updates for everyone
Skipping feature updates entirely
scenarios.hint: Who should meet the new update first: 10 volunteers or 300 users?
scenarios.prompt: What deployment discipline would have caught this?
scenarios.situation: A feature update was assigned to the 'All Devices' group directly. It broke a line-of-business app on 300 machines overnight.
scenarios.title: The ring that skipped pilot
scenarios.why: Update rings exist to stage risk: a small pilot ring validates the update against real apps, then broader rings follow on a schedule. Assigning an untested feature update to All Devices skips the entire safety mechanism. The ring structure is the process, not just a setting.

choices: Install the sensor manually on each device
Deploy the Defender for Endpoint onboarding policy from Intune (endpoint security > EDR) to the device groups — Intune handles onboarding automatically
Onboarding happens automatically with no policy
Reimage the devices with a Defender-enabled image
scenarios.hint: Which Intune blade exists specifically to onboard devices to EDR?
scenarios.prompt: How do you onboard Intune-managed devices to Defender for Endpoint?
scenarios.situation: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint shows 200 Intune-managed devices as 'not onboarded.' The EDR sensor was never deployed to them.
scenarios.title: Defender onboarding
scenarios.why: Intune's endpoint security EDR onboarding policy pushes the Defender for Endpoint onboarding configuration to managed devices — no manual installs, no reimaging. The Intune-Defender connector syncs device state, and the security center reflects onboarding within hours.

choices: Enable in block mode immediately — security first
Start in audit mode, review the events to find legitimate processes that would be blocked, create exclusions, then switch to block mode
ASR rules cannot be tested — deploy and hope
Disable Office macros instead
scenarios.hint: How do you learn what a rule would break without breaking it?
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe rollout approach for ASR rules?
scenarios.situation: An attack surface reduction rule 'Block Office applications from creating child processes' is proposed. Security fears it will break legitimate macros on day one.
scenarios.title: ASR rule in audit
scenarios.why: ASR rules support audit mode precisely for this: they log what would have been blocked without blocking it. Reviewing audit events reveals legitimate line-of-business processes needing exclusions before enforcement. Flipping straight to block is how security projects earn their reputation for breaking payroll.

choices: BitLocker cannot be recovered — the data is lost by design
The Intune BitLocker policy should have enforced encryption AND escrowed recovery keys to Microsoft Entra ID — check the device's page in Intune/Entra for the stored key
Email the user for the key they memorized
Disable BitLocker to avoid this in future
scenarios.hint: Where should a managed encryption key live besides the device?
scenarios.prompt: What should the BitLocker policy have ensured, and where do you look now?
scenarios.situation: A laptop's motherboard failed and BitLocker recovery is triggered. Nobody knows the 48-digit recovery key, and the device was encrypted manually by its user.
scenarios.title: BitLocker keys in the wind
scenarios.why: A proper Intune BitLocker policy does two things: requires encryption and escrows the recovery key to Microsoft Entra ID automatically. Recovery then means opening the device record and reading the stored key — no memorization, no sticky notes. Manual per-user encryption without escrow is exactly how keys end up 'in the wind.'

choices: Wipe both — consistency matters
Retire the personal phone (removes corporate data and unenrolls, leaves personal data) and Wipe or Autopilot Reset the corporate laptop (full reset for the next user)
Retire both — wipe is never appropriate
Do nothing — the accounts are disabled anyway
scenarios.hint: Which action knows the difference between corporate and personal data?
scenarios.prompt: Which remote action fits each device?
scenarios.situation: Two departures: (1) a contractor's personal phone with corporate email via app protection, no enrollment; (2) a corporate laptop being recycled to a new hire.
scenarios.title: Retire vs wipe
scenarios.why: Retire is the surgical option: removes company data, app protection policies, and the Intune enrollment while leaving personal photos and apps alone — the BYOD-appropriate action. Wipe factory-resets the whole device, right for corporate-owned hardware changing hands. Matching the action to ownership is the privacy-respecting, exam-tested distinction.

choices: Compliance policies take 24 hours to apply — wait
Compliance policies evaluate and report health (compliant/noncompliant); enforcing settings like PIN length is the job of configuration profiles — the admin used the wrong policy type
PIN policies are not supported in Intune
The policy needs a user group instead of a device group
scenarios.hint: Which policy type changes device settings, and which only judges them?
scenarios.prompt: What is the conceptual error?
scenarios.situation: A junior admin created a 'compliance policy' requiring a 6-digit PIN, expecting Intune to enforce the PIN on devices. Nothing changed on the endpoints.
scenarios.title: Compliance vs configuration
scenarios.why: Compliance = measurement: it checks state (encrypted? PIN present? OS current?) and reports a verdict that Conditional Access can consume. Configuration = enforcement: configuration profiles actually set the PIN length, password rules, and restrictions. The admin measured when they meant to configure.

choices: Whichever policy was created first
The co-management workload slider — each workload (compliance policies, device configuration, etc.) is assigned to ConfigMgr or Intune, and can be piloted to Intune for a test collection first
Intune always wins in co-management
Delete ConfigMgr
scenarios.hint: Which control assigns each workload to an authority?
scenarios.prompt: What decides which authority wins for a workload?
scenarios.situation: Devices are co-managed by Configuration Manager and Intune. Compliance policies were created in Intune, but ConfigMgr keeps winning and the Intune policies never apply.
scenarios.title: Co-management tug of war
scenarios.why: Co-management splits authority per workload via the slider: compliance policies, device configuration, Windows Update, and others each point at ConfigMgr or Intune. Piloting moves a workload to Intune for one collection while the rest stay put — the safe migration path. Without moving the slider, the Intune policies sit idle.

choices: The .intunewin file is too large
The detection rule is wrong — Intune uses it to decide if the app is already installed, and a bad rule fails the install immediately; fix the file/registry detection logic
Win32 apps cannot deploy to Windows 11
The devices need the Company Portal first
evidence:
Status: Failed
Error: detection rule mismatch (0x87D1041C)
scenarios.hint: How does Intune know whether the install actually worked?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely packaging error?
scenarios.situation: A Win32 app packaged with the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool deploys to 50 devices but reports 'failed' on all of them within seconds — too fast for a real install attempt.
scenarios.title: The IntuneWin that wouldn't install
scenarios.why: Detection rules tell Intune how to recognize a successful install (file exists, registry key, MSI product code). A rule that never matches — wrong path, wrong version check — makes every install 'fail' instantly because Intune concludes the app is not present after setup. The error code and the instant failure are the signature.

choices: Assign both as Available — users choose everything
VPN client as Required (auto-installs, enforced), PDF reader as Available (shown in Company Portal for self-service install)
Assign both as Required — optional is not a real assignment
Email the installers to everyone
scenarios.hint: Which assignment installs with no user action?
scenarios.prompt: How do you assign each app in Intune?
scenarios.situation: The VPN client must be on every corporate laptop with no exceptions. The PDF reader is optional — users install it if they want it.
scenarios.title: Required vs available
scenarios.why: Required assignments push the app automatically and keep it installed — the enforcement mechanism for must-have software. Available assignments publish to the Company Portal for voluntary install — the self-service model. Uninstall assignments remove. Matching assignment intent to business need is core app lifecycle management.

choices: Configuration profiles — they work without enrollment
App protection policies (MAM) — they protect corporate data inside managed apps (Outlook, Teams) on unenrolled devices, with selective wipe of just the corporate data
Conditional Access alone
BitLocker policies for mobile
scenarios.hint: Which policy type draws the boundary around the app instead of the device?
scenarios.prompt: Which Intune capability delivers this without enrollment?
scenarios.situation: Executives refuse device enrollment on personal phones but need corporate email with copy/paste restrictions and remote wipe of corporate data only.
scenarios.title: MAM without enrollment
scenarios.why: App protection policies (mobile application management) apply at the app layer: PIN on the app, block copy/paste to personal apps, encrypt corporate data, and selective-wipe only the corporate container — no device enrollment, no device wipe. This is the standard answer for 'protect the data, not the device' on BYOD.

choices: Sideload .appx files via USB
Use the new Microsoft Store app type in Intune (Winget-based) — browse and add Store apps directly, assign like any other app
Store apps can no longer be managed
Email users the Store link
scenarios.hint: Which package manager underpins the new Store integration?
scenarios.prompt: What is the current approach for Store apps in Intune?
scenarios.situation: The old Microsoft Store for Business is retired. The team needs to deploy a Store app to managed devices through Intune with the current supported method.
scenarios.title: The Store app shuffle
scenarios.why: Intune's new Microsoft Store app type (built on the Winget repository) replaced the retired Store for Business integration: admins search the Store catalog inside Intune, add the app, and assign it with the same Required/Available model. No sideloading, no private store portal needed for public apps.

choices: Assign v3 as Available and hope users switch
Configure supersedence: v3 supersedes v2, so Intune upgrades devices automatically (installing v3 and uninstalling v2 per the supersedence rules)
Delete v2 from Intune — deletion uninstalls everywhere
Supersedence only works for Store apps
scenarios.hint: Which feature tells Intune that v3 replaces v2?
scenarios.prompt: Which Intune relationship handles the upgrade?
scenarios.situation: Version 3 of the in-house app is ready. Version 2 is installed on 400 devices as Required. IT wants v3 to replace v2 automatically without manual uninstalls.
scenarios.title: Supersedence
scenarios.why: Supersedence links app versions: when v3 supersedes v2, Intune's upgrade logic installs the new version and removes the old one according to the relationship settings. Deleting v2 from the console would orphan or unexpectedly remove it; Available assignment relies on users. Supersedence works for Win32 apps — the main version-churn case.

choices: Group Policy on the phones
App configuration policies — deliver key-value settings (server URL, signature) to managed apps, for both enrolled devices and MAM-managed apps
Email the settings to each user
Configuration profiles — they configure apps directly
scenarios.hint: Which policy type speaks to the app rather than the OS?
scenarios.prompt: How do you push settings into the app?
scenarios.situation: The managed Outlook app needs the corporate mail server URL and a default signature preconfigured on every managed device — users should not type settings by hand.
scenarios.title: App config for managed apps
scenarios.why: App configuration policies inject settings into managed apps via key-value pairs the app understands — server URLs, default signatures, branding. They target managed devices or managed apps (MAM), covering both enrolled and unenrolled scenarios. Configuration profiles configure the OS/device, not inside apps.

choices: Package it as a Win32 app with a dummy installer
Add it as a Web link app type in Intune — it publishes the URL to the Company Portal with the icon, and Entra SSO handles sign-in
Web apps cannot appear in the Company Portal
Create a bookmarks email
scenarios.hint: Which app type deploys a URL instead of a binary?
scenarios.prompt: How do you deploy it through Intune?
scenarios.situation: The company intranet (a web app with Microsoft Entra SSO) should appear on users' Company Portal and Start menus like a deployed app, but there is nothing to install.
scenarios.title: The web link that needed SSO
scenarios.why: The Web link app type exists exactly for this: publish a URL with an icon and description to the Company Portal (and optionally Start menu) with zero installer. Because sign-in flows through Microsoft Entra SSO, users get one-click access. Wrapping it as Win32 adds pointless packaging overhead.

foundations.why_needed: MD-102 assumes you can instantly tell the three device identities apart: Microsoft Entra joined (corporate-owned, cloud-native, Intune-managed), hybrid Microsoft Entra joined (domain-joined on-premises plus cloud identity via Microsoft Entra Connect sync), and Microsoft Entra registered (personal/BYOD — a work account on a personal device, app-level management only). Join type decides everything downstream: which enrollment path works, which Conditional Access controls apply, and whether retire or wipe is the safe remote action. When in doubt, run dsregcmd /status: AzureAdJoined + DomainJoined + MdmUrl tell the whole story.

checks.hint: In the Terminal tab, run `dsregcmd /status`. If the check fails, confirm you typed it exactly and that the output contains "AzureAdJoined".

concepts: Windows Autopilot registers devices by hardware hash (collected via the Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo script or by the reseller) and matches them to a deployment profile at the out-of-box experience.

Autopilot deployment profiles define the OOBE: user-driven for standard users, self-deploying for kiosks and shared devices with no user interaction — and they must target device groups, since no user is signed in yet.
Provisioning packages (.ppkg) from Windows Configuration Designer apply settings offline from USB — the answer for sites without reliable cloud connectivity.
Autopilot Reset is the device-handoff action: strips user data, keeps Autopilot registration, re-runs OOBE. Retire unenrolls; Wipe factory-resets.

Modern provisioning replaces golden images: ship the OEM image, let Autopilot + Intune layer apps, policies, and settings dynamically per group. Subscription activation steps Pro up to Enterprise via Microsoft 365 licensing.

example.code:
Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo.ps1 -OutputFile C:\temp\hashes.csv
# Import hashes.csv → Intune → Devices → Windows enrollment → Devices
example.walkthrough: The community script exports each device's hardware hash to CSV; importing it registers the devices in Autopilot, after which an assigned deployment profile takes over at first boot.

pitfalls: Common trap: assigning Autopilot profiles to user groups — no user exists at OOBE time.
Common trap: expecting Autopilot to work offline — it requires cloud connectivity.
Common trap: using Wipe when Autopilot Reset preserves registration and is faster.
Common trap: forgetting the Enrollment Status Page will block on a failing app.
lessons.title: Deploy Windows Client — Core concepts
lessons.try_it: Trace an Autopilot flow in the Terminal tab →

concepts: Three device identities: Microsoft Entra joined (corporate, managed), hybrid Entra joined (on-premises domain + cloud), Entra registered (personal/BYOD, work account only).
Automatic MDM enrollment is a separate switch: Entra ID > Mobility (MDM and MAM) > MDM user scope set to Microsoft Intune — without it, joined devices never reach Intune.
Conditional Access combines signals (user, device, location, app, risk) with grant controls (require MFA, require compliant device, block). Named locations represent trusted office networks.
Compliance policies measure device health (encryption, OS version, Defender state) and report compliant/noncompliant; Actions for noncompliance escalate from user notification to lock or retire.

Always exclude break-glass emergency accounts from Conditional Access policies so a misconfiguration can never lock out all administrators. dsregcmd /status is the on-device ground truth for join and enrollment state.

example.code:
dsregcmd /status
AzureAdJoined : YES
DomainJoined  : NO
MdmUrl        : https://enrollment.manage.microsoft.com/...
example.walkthrough: YES/NO/present-MdmUrl reads as: Entra joined, not hybrid, and enrolled in Intune. A blank MdmUrl with AzureAdJoined YES means the join worked but enrollment did not — check the MDM user scope.

pitfalls: Common trap: assuming Entra join implies Intune enrollment — they are separate steps.
Common trap: targeting Autopilot/ESP policies at user groups instead of device groups.
Common trap: a compliance policy with no actions — a verdict without consequences.
Common trap: forgetting break-glass exclusions in Conditional Access.
lessons.title: Manage Identity & Compliance — Core concepts
lessons.try_it: Read a dsregcmd output in the Terminal tab →

concepts: Update rings (Windows Update for Business) control deferrals, deadlines, and grace periods: deadlines enforce, grace periods give users a humane window before forced restart, active hours protect the workday. Roll out in rings: pilot first, then broad.

Defender for Endpoint onboarding for Intune devices is a policy (endpoint security > EDR), not a manual install. ASR rules should start in audit mode — review what would block, add exclusions, then enforce.
BitLocker policy must both require encryption and escrow recovery keys to Microsoft Entra ID, or a dead motherboard becomes a data-loss event.

Remote actions: Retire removes corporate data and unenrolls (BYOD-safe); Wipe factory-resets (corporate-owned handoff); Autopilot Reset re-provisions for the next user; Remote lock, Restart, and Sync cover the rest.

Compliance policies judge health; configuration profiles enforce settings. In co-management, the workload slider decides whether ConfigMgr or Intune owns each workload — pilot workloads to Intune per collection.

example.code:
Update ring: Pilot
Feature deferral: 7 days | Quality deferral: 3 days
Deadline: 5 days | Grace period: 2 days
example.walkthrough: Pilot devices get updates slightly delayed for validation; the 5-day deadline enforces installation and the 2-day grace period lets users pick their reboot moment before the device insists.

pitfalls: Common trap: zero grace period — forced reboots mid-presentation.
Common trap: assigning an untested update to All Devices instead of a pilot ring.
Common trap: manual BitLocker with no key escrow.
Common trap: using Wipe on a personal device — Retire is the BYOD-safe action.
lessons.title: Manage & Protect Devices — Core concepts
lessons.try_it: Check BitLocker and update status in the Terminal tab →

concepts: Win32 apps are packaged with the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool into .intunewin; detection rules (file, registry, MSI product code) tell Intune whether the install succeeded — a bad rule fails instantly.
Assignments: Required auto-installs and enforces; Available publishes to the Company Portal for self-service; Uninstall removes. Match the assignment to the business need.
App protection policies (MAM) guard corporate data inside apps on unenrolled BYOD devices: app PIN, copy/paste restrictions, selective wipe of only corporate data.
Supersedence links app versions so v3 automatically replaces v2. App configuration policies push key-value settings (server URLs, signatures) into managed apps.
The new Microsoft Store app type (Winget-based) replaced Store for Business; the Web link type publishes SSO web apps to the Company Portal with no installer.

example.code:
IntuneWinAppUtil.exe -c C:\source\app -s setup.exe -o C:\output
# → app.intunewin + detection rule: File C:\Program Files\App\app.exe exists
example.walkthrough: The prep tool wraps the installer into .intunewin; the detection rule gives Intune its success criterion. If the rule's path is wrong, every deployment fails in seconds — the classic detection-rule mismatch.

pitfalls: Common trap: wrong detection rule path — instant failures across the fleet.
Common trap: assigning must-have apps as Available and wondering why nobody has them.
Common trap: enrolling BYOD devices when MAM app protection was sufficient.
Common trap: deleting an old version instead of using supersedence.

simulations.brief: A batch of Autopilot devices hangs on the Enrollment Status Page and eventually times out. Users cannot get to the desktop. Work the evidence in order.
simulations.debrief: You separated ESP blocking failures from profile assignment gaps — the two most common Autopilot stall causes.

evidence:
ESP phase: Device setup
Status: Failed
Failing step: Installing apps (1 of 3)
App: ContosoLOB.msi (2.1 GB)
steps.explain: ESP waits for its blocking apps; a failing installer fails the whole setup phase. Removing the app from ESP's blocking list (or fixing the installer) unblocks provisioning — the app can retry post-enrollment. Longer timeouts just delay the same failure.
options: Extend the ESP timeout to 120 minutes
Remove or fix the blocking app — a failing 2.1 GB MSI holds ESP until timeout; take it out of the ESP blocking list so setup completes
Re-register all hardware hashes
Disable ESP for the tenant
steps.symptom: Devices time out on ESP; no profile errors shown.

evidence:
20 devices: Profile status = Not assigned
Group: AP-Laptops (device group, 40 members)
steps.explain: The devices sit in a device group with no profile assigned to it — assignment is explicit, not automatic. Targeting the deployment profile at the AP-Laptops device group gives every member its OOBE configuration. Converting to a user group would make it worse: no user exists at OOBE time.
options: Assign the deployment profile to the AP-Laptops device group — profiles must target device groups, and these devices were never assigned
Wait 24 hours for automatic assignment
Convert the device group to a user group
Reimage the unassigned devices
steps.symptom: With the app unblocked, half the devices now fail with 'no Autopilot profile assigned.'

simulations.title: Stuck at 'Setting up your device'

simulations.brief: Monday 9 AM: the helpdesk is flooded — every user gets 'access denied' opening Outlook. A Conditional Access policy changed Friday. Work the evidence in order.
simulations.debrief: You practiced the CA incident loop: report-only to stop the bleeding, sign-in logs for data, then re-scope the policy to match device reality.

evidence:
CA-Email-Health (modified Friday 6:12 PM)
Target: All users, Exchange Online
Grant: Require device to be marked as compliant
Enforcement: On
steps.explain: Requiring compliant devices when half the fleet is noncompliant (or never evaluated) is an instant lockout. Report-only mode stops the bleeding while keeping the policy visible for testing; deleting destroys the audit trail. First establish the compliance coverage, then phase enforcement.
options: Delete the policy immediately
The policy now requires compliant devices for all users — check what fraction of devices are actually compliant before deciding; put the policy in report-only mode while investigating
Force a password reset for all users
Disable MFA tenant-wide
steps.symptom: All users blocked from Exchange Online with an access-denied / CA error.

steps.explain: The policy's intent (healthy devices for email) is right, but the scope ignored BYOD reality. The mature design: require compliant device for managed devices, and require approved app + app protection policy for personal ones. Report-only mode gave you the data to scope correctly instead of guessing.
options: Enforce anyway — security first
Scope the policy: target managed/corporate devices for the compliance grant and pair it with app protection policies (MAM) for personal devices, so BYOD keeps email with app-level protection
Remove the grant control entirely
Block personal devices permanently
steps.symptom: In report-only mode, sign-in logs show 60% of devices would be blocked — most are personal phones that were never enrolled.

simulations.title: Nobody can open email

simulations.brief: The pilot update ring was supposed to receive the new Windows feature update two weeks ago. Pilot devices still report the old build. Work the evidence in order.
simulations.debrief: You separated policy causes (deferral hiding the update) from device causes (disk full) — the two halves of update troubleshooting.

evidence:
Feature update deferral: 180 days
Servicing channel: General Availability
Pilot devices: last check-in 2 hours ago, compliant
steps.explain: Feature deferral delays when the update is even offered: 180 days means the ring will not see it for six months. For a pilot meant to validate now, the deferral must be small (days, not months). Devices checking in fine rules out connectivity — the policy is simply telling them to wait.
options: The 180-day feature deferral is still hiding the update — reduce the deferral so the update becomes offerable
Restart the Windows Update service on each device
Reassign the devices to the broad ring
The servicing channel is wrong — switch to Insider
steps.symptom: Pilot devices show no feature update offered after two weeks.

evidence: Error 0x80070070: DISK_FULL — 3.2 GB free, ~10 GB needed
steps.explain: 0x80070070 is the classic disk-full error during the download/expand phase. Feature updates need significant free space; the fix is operational (clean up, external storage, or Files On-Demand policies) not policy timing. Deadlines and deferrals cannot create disk space.
options: Increase the deadline — more time fixes disk space
Free disk space (Disk Cleanup, remove old profiles) — 0x80070070 is ERROR_DISK_FULL; feature updates need roughly 10 GB free
Defer the update again
Disable the update ring
steps.symptom: With deferral fixed, updates download but fail at 71% with 0x80070070.

simulations.title: The feature update that never lands
